title: Handling tool errors and edge cases
notes: When a tool fails, send back a tool_result with is_error true and a clear message, so the model can recover.
Never swallow an error into an empty string: the model reads silence as success and fills the gap with a guess.
Retry temporary failures with backoff, cap the loop with a step limit, and when stuck, tell the customer honestly or hand off.

slides.title: Handling tool errors and edge cases
slides.sub: What Scout should do when a tool fails, so it never fills the gap with a guess
sentences: Remember Elena, whose rope Scout called delivered while it was still on a truck?
That was not a bad model; it was a tool error that got hidden.
In this lesson you will see how to report errors to the model, when to retry, and when to stop and say so.

slides.title: What went wrong for Elena

messages.label: Elena
messages.text: Has my rope arrived yet? Order ORB-10560.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Good news, your rope has been delivered!

aside.label: The real bug
aside.text: An empty result looks like nothing to report, so the model filled the silence with the likeliest story.

sentences: Here is the conversation from the hook, one message at a time.
Elena asks whether her climbing rope has arrived.
Scout calls track parcel with her tracking number.
ParcelPath times out, and the code catches the error and returns an empty string.
From where the model sits, the tool worked and simply had nothing new to say.
So it writes the likeliest ending to the story: delivered.
The model did not lie on purpose; the code hid the one fact it needed, that the lookup had failed.

slides.title: Swallowing an error versus reporting it

left.label: Swallowed
points: The model sees an empty, normal result

right.label: Reported
points: The model knows that it doesn't know
It retries, explains, or hands off

sentences: There are two ways to handle a tool that fails.
The first is to swallow it: catch the error and return an empty string, or some default value.
It feels tidy, but it hides the failure from the model, and from you.
The second is to report it: send back a tool result marked as an error, with a clear message.
Now the model knows that it does not know.
It can try another way, explain the delay honestly, or hand the question to a person.

slides.title: Reporting an error in the tool loop
slides.lead: The loop from this module catches any tool failure and sends it back, marked as an error.

rows.out: Says what went wrong, in words
Tells the model this call failed
Errors go back with the other results

aside.label: Write it for the model
aside.text: Say what failed and what is now unknown, for example: ParcelPath timed out, status unknown.

sentences: In code, the fix is a few lines in the tool loop you already have.
The try block runs the tool, and if anything goes wrong, the except block catches it.
Instead of hiding the error, you write it into the result's content, in words.
And you set the is error flag to true, which tells the model this call failed.
The error goes back in the same user message as any other results, so every request still gets an answer.
Make the message useful to the model: say what failed, and what is now unknown.

slides.title: Which errors are worth a retry?

cells: Report now; ask the customer to check
Report now and alert the team

note.text: Retry what might work next time. Report what won't, straight away.

sentences: Some errors are worth a second try, and some are not.
A timeout is usually temporary, so retry, waiting a little longer each time.
A four twenty-nine means slow down, so wait as long as the API asks, then retry.
Server errors in the five hundreds are often brief, so a couple of retries is reasonable.
But a four oh four, tracking number not found, will fail the same way every time, so report it straight away.
And a four oh one, a bad API key, needs a person on your team, not another attempt.
Retry what might work next time, and report what will not.

slides.title: Retrying with backoff
slides.lead: Retries live inside the tool, where your code handles them quietly. Then it gives up, loudly.

rows.out: Then fail clearly; the loop reports it

aside.label: A customer is waiting
aside.text: Three tries with a ten-second timeout is already half a minute. Keep retries few and short.

sentences: Retries belong inside the tool, where your code can handle them quietly.
Try the call up to three times.
Catch only the temporary errors, like a timeout, and let everything else fail at once.
Between tries, wait a little longer each time, which is called backoff, so a struggling server gets room to recover.
If the last try fails too, raise a clear error, and the tool loop reports it to the model with the is error flag.
Keep the total short, because a customer is waiting while you retry.

slides.title: Edge cases to plan for
slides.lead: Errors aren't the only surprises. Plan for these before customers find them.

bullets.text: Endless loops: cap the tool loop with MAX_STEPS
Missing input: no order number, so ask instead of guessing
Bad arguments or unknown tool: report it as an error too
Huge results: trim them before they reach the model

aside.label: Why a step limit
aside.text: A failing tool can make the model try again and again. MAX_STEPS stops the loop, and the bill.

sentences: Errors are not the only surprises, so plan for a few edge cases too.
The model might keep calling tools, so the loop always has a step limit, and Scout's is six.
A customer might not give an order number, and the right move is to ask, not to call a tool with a guess.
The model might send arguments your function rejects, and that is reported as an error too, so it can correct itself.
And a tool might return far too much, which you trim, as you saw in the last lesson.
The step limit matters most: a failing tool can make the model try again and again, and every try costs money.

slides.title: Telling the customer honestly

messages.label: track_parcel · is_error
messages.text: Error: ParcelPath timed out 3 times. Status unknown.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: I can't reach our carrier's tracking right now, so I can't confirm where your rope is. Shall I pass this to our support team? They can check with the carrier directly.

messages.label: Elena
messages.text: Yes please. Thanks for being straight with me.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Done. I've passed on your order number and question, and the team will reply by email.

sentences: When the retries are used up, the last step is honesty.
The tool result says ParcelPath timed out three times, and the status is unknown.
Scout tells Elena exactly that, in plain words, without guessing where the parcel is.
Then it offers something useful: a person who can check with the carrier directly.
Elena says yes, and an honest answer keeps her trust, where a wrong delivered lost it.
Scout passes on her question, using a hand-off tool you will add in Module 5.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: Report tool failures as a tool_result with is_error true
Never return an empty string: the model will guess
Retry temporary errors with backoff; report the rest at once
Cap the steps; when stuck, say so honestly or hand off

sentences: Let us pull the module together.
When a tool fails, send the error back as a tool result marked as an error, with a clear message.
Never swallow it into an empty string, because the model will fill the gap with a guess.
Retry temporary failures with backoff, and report the rest straight away.
Cap the loop's steps, and when Scout is stuck, it says so honestly or hands off to a person.
Next, watch Scout call its first tools, then build your own in the guided practice.

midQuiz.q: Why did Scout tell Elena her rope was delivered?
options: ParcelPath sent a wrong status for her parcel
The tool hid a timeout by returning an empty string, so the model guessed
The model misread her tracking number
midQuiz.explain: The timeout was caught and turned into an empty string. To the model that looked like a normal, empty result, so it filled the gap.
midQuiz.hint: What did the model actually receive from track_parcel?

midQuiz.q: Which of these errors is worth retrying?
midQuiz.explain: A timeout is often temporary, so a short retry with backoff may succeed. A 404 or 401 will fail the same way every time.
midQuiz.hint: Which one might work if you simply tried again in a second?

endQuiz.q: A tool fails with an exception. What should go back to the model?
options: Nothing: skip the tool_result for that call
A tool_result with is_error true and a clear message
An empty tool_result, so the model carries on
endQuiz.explain: Every tool request needs a matching tool_result. Mark failures with is_error and say what went wrong, so the model can recover.
endQuiz.hint: The model asked a question. What does it need to hear, even when the news is bad?

endQuiz.q: ParcelPath has been down for twenty minutes and Elena is waiting in the chat. What should Scout do?
options: Keep retrying until ParcelPath comes back
Say it can't check right now, and offer to hand off to a person
Tell her the rope has probably been delivered by now
endQuiz.explain: Retries are for brief blips, not outages. Being honest about what Scout can't check, plus a clear next step, keeps the customer's trust.
endQuiz.hint: Is twenty minutes a blip? And what does Elena need from Scout right now?
